units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. We're at the last stop. Is that it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the front of the Rubens House.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In Dutch, the Rubenshuis. It's on the Wapper, which used to be called Vaartstraat.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And this was his house?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1610, Rubens bought the property.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A year earlier, in 1609, he'd married Isabella Brant.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he rebuilt it in the style of an Italian palace.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A palace in Antwerp.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With a studio, a portico, a courtyard, and a Baroque garden.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So he wasn't just a painter. He was a developer.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A very successful painter, with a studio full of students and assistants.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A lot of his famous works came out of here.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it was a workshop.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A workshop, a home and a showroom in one.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He lived here for most of his life, until he died in 1640.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened to it after?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His widow, Helena Fourment, leased the house to William Cavendish and his wife Margaret.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After Margaret left in 1660, the house was sold.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And how did it end up a museum?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A legacy from an architect named Henri Blomme helped the city buy the house in 1937.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Good for him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And after extensive restoration, it opened as a museum in 1946, with period furniture and works by Rubens and his contemporaries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Can we go in?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This is where I have to be careful.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the time of writing, the main section, the artist's residence, is closed for renovation.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So please check the official website before you plan on going inside.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And if it's closed?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look at the outside, and think about the garden.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The courtyard opens onto the Baroque garden Rubens planned himself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Behind it is the Rubenianum, a study center and archive for scholars.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right. So even if the house is shut, we've got the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the four paintings in the cathedral.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you went inside earlier, you've already seen Rubens at work.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What else should we know about him?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He led the Antwerp school of painting in the 17th century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Another painter, Anthony van Dyck, belongs to the same school.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Rubens is buried in Saint James's church.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you have time left, ask for directions and check the hours.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the city around his house.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did it look like in his day?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Poorer than in the golden age.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The river was closed after he died, in 1648.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the art, the printing, and the sense of itself as a great city stayed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So Rubens was at the end of the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Rather the middle of the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city came back, later, in a different way.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. I think we need to do the tally.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Go on.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The hand in the river. The hand on the fountain.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The printers' hands. The painter's hands.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's four. I won.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You said more than one giant hand.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You got one in the legend, one on the fountain.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Technically, yes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'll take it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Pause here. Look at the house.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Walk through the doorway, if you can.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then one more thing, a drink. You said you'd been good.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I've been very good.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's a champagne bar called the Laurent-Perrier Champagne Bar, at Meir 78, inside the old Stadsfeestzaal shopping building.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a few minutes' walk from here, on the same shopping street.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Champagne. At last.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Check its opening hours first.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was listed as open until 6:30 in the evening on the day we looked, but hours change.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And I can't promise it serves cocktails.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you want a cocktail with a view, there's a small bar called Jones and Co, on Pelgrimstraat, with a terrace that looks toward the cathedral.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Again, check hours.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A toast to Rubens.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A toast to Rubens.
